translations.text: "The former treatise have I made," and the rest.
Luke the Evangelist admonished us in this epistle reading, saying thus: "The Saviour, the Redeemer of the world, showed himself alive to his disciples
after his passion and his resurrection, in many proofs, over forty days, and spoke to them about the kingdom of God, eating together with them;
and he commanded them not to depart from the city of Jerusalem, but to wait there for his Father's promise, 'which,' he said, 'you have heard from my mouth.'
"For John the Baptist baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit now, after a few days.
Then the assembly of his disciples said with one mind, 'Dear Lord, will you now set the end of this world?'
He answered them, 'It is not for you to know the time or the moment that my Father has set by his power;
but you shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit, and you shall be my witnesses in the land of Judea, and in all the world, to the farthest land.'
And he then led them out of the city up to a mountain which is called the Mount of Olives, and blessed them with uplifted hands.
Then with that blessing he went to heaven while they looked on; and the heavenly cloud bent down toward him and took him from their sight."
"As they stood gazing up to heaven, they saw there two angels in white garments, saying thus: 'You men of Galilee, why do you stand gazing thus toward heaven?
The Saviour, who has now been taken from your sight into heaven, will come again just as you saw him ascend into heaven.'

Then they returned to the city of Jerusalem with great joy, and went up into an upper room, and remained there until Pentecost in prayers and in praises of God, until the Holy Spirit came to them, just as the noble King had promised them before."

"In this company were Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, the other James and Simon, the other Judas, and Mary the mother of the Saviour, and various others, both men and women.
The whole company was a hundred and twenty people, continuing with one mind in prayer."
The Saviour taught the holy doctrine to his disciples before his passion, and after his resurrection he remained among them for forty days,

from the holy Easter season until this present day. In many ways he rebuked and tested his disciples, and repeated what he had taught them before, so that they would have full teaching and right faith.
He ate after his resurrection, not because he needed earthly food any longer, but so that he would show that his body was real.
He ate through his power, not out of need. Just as fire consumes a drop of water, so Christ's divine power consumed the food he had eaten.
Truly, after the general resurrection our bodies will need no strengthening from earthly food, but the Saviour will supply all our needs with heavenly things,
and we will be enriched with glory, and able to do whatever pleases us, and we will be very swift to travel throughout all the wide expanses of God's kingdom.
He promised his disciples now and often that he would send them the Holy Spirit, and said thus: "When he comes, he will instruct you and guide you in all the things that I have told you."
Then the Holy Spirit came in the form of fire to the holy household on the eleventh day after Christ's ascension, and kindled them all with a fire that did no harm,
and they were filled with the heavenly teaching, and knew all the languages of the world, and fearlessly preached faith and baptism to the powerful and the cruel.
The holy company asked Christ whether he would bring this world to an end at that time. He said to them in answer, "It is not for you to know the time that my Father has set by his own power."
He also said in another place, "No one knows the day or the time of the ending of this world, neither the angels nor any saint, but God alone."
Nevertheless, by the signs that Christ spoke of, we see that the ending is very near, though it is unknown to us.

The apostles were witnesses of Christ's works, because they preached his passion, his resurrection and his ascension, first to the Jewish people. Afterwards their voice went out to every land, and their words to the ends of the whole world.
because they wrote down Christ's miracles, and those books endure among Christian people, both where the apostles preached in person and where they never came.
All creatures serve their Creator. When Christ was born, heaven sent a new star, which announced God's birth.
Again, when he ascended to heaven, the heavenly cloud bowed down toward him and received him:
not that the cloud carried him, for he holds the throne of the heavens, but he went with the cloud out of the sight of men. Two angels in white garments were seen there then.
Angels were likewise seen at his birth, but the holy gospel did not make clear how they were adorned, because God came to us very humbly.
At his ascension angels were seen adorned with white garments. Joy is signified by white clothing, because Christ went from here with great joy and with great majesty.
At his birth it seemed as if the Godhead were humbled, and at his ascension the humanity was exalted and glorified.
By his ascension the handwritten bond of our condemnation is blotted out, and the sentence of our corruption is reversed.
When Adam had sinned, the Almighty Ruler said to him, "You are earth, and you shall return to earth.
You are dust, and you shall return to dust." Now today that same nature went, incorruptible, into the kingdom of heaven.
The two angels said that Christ will come in the same way as he went up, because at the great judgement he will be seen in human form, so that those who killed him can recognize him.
…who had earlier put him to death, and also those who despised his teaching, so that they will then justly receive the eternal punishment with the devil.
Holy Scripture says, "Tollatur impius ne uideat gloriam Dei": "Let the sight of God's glory be taken away from the wicked."
The wicked, who despised him earlier in life, will not see Christ's glory; rather, they will then see as terrible the one whom they scorned as humble.
"As the eleven disciples were sitting at table," and so on. We have now read Luke's account of Christ's ascension; now we turn our study to the other evangelist, Mark, who said in this day's gospel
that the Saviour showed himself to his apostles and rebuked them, because at first they would not believe in his resurrection from death when it was made known to them.
Then the Lord said to his disciples, "Go throughout all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; whoever does not believe will be condemned.
These signs will follow those who believe," etc. This gospel has now been told simply, but now, following Gregory's commentary, we will reveal its hidden meaning to you.
The apostles' doubt about Christ's resurrection was not so much their unbelief as our strengthening.
Those who believed quickly helped us less than those who doubted, because the doubters looked at and touched the scars of Christ's wounds, and so drove all doubts from our hearts.
The Saviour rebuked his disciples' doubt when he was about to leave them in the body, so that they would remember the words that he spoke to them at his departure.
He said then, "Go throughout all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature."

The gospel is for us to hear, and it is very much to be loved: that we may escape the punishment of hell and its cruel torments through the Saviour's humanity, and come to the host of angels through his humility.
He said, "Preach to every creature": but by that name man alone is meant. Stones are creatures, but they have no life, nor do they feel.
Grass and trees live without feeling. They do not live through a soul, but through their greenness.
Beasts live and have feeling, but without reason: they have no reason, because they are without souls.
Angels live, and feel, and reason. Now man has something of all creatures.
He has in common with stones that he exists; he has in common with trees that he lives; with animals, that he feels; with angels, that he understands.
Now man is called 'all creation,' because he has something in common with all creation.
The gospel is preached to all creation when it is preached to man alone, because all earthly things are created for man alone, and they all have some likeness to man, as we said before.
"He who believes and is baptized will be saved; and he who does not believe will be condemned."
Faith is true when a man does not deny by perverse conduct what he believes; about this John the apostle said, "He who says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar."
Again the apostle James says, "The faith that is without good works is dead."
Again he said, "What good does it do you to have faith if you do not have good works?
Faith cannot save you without works. Devils believe, but they tremble."
The devils saw Christ in this life, in his human nature, and they fell at his feet and cried out and said, "You are the Son of God; you have come because you would destroy us."
The person who will not believe in God and has no fear of God is worse than the devil.
The person who believes and has fear, but still will not do good, is like the devils.
In a certain treatise, which is thought to have been Saint Hilary's, we find it written thus, as we have translated it here into English, and we have set down the Latin itself as testimony:

"Demons believe and tremble; but he who does not believe and does not tremble is worse than the demons; and he who believes and trembles, but does not carry out the truth in works, is like the demons."

The person who believes rightly, lives his life rightly, and does good works in the fear of God until the end of his life will be saved, and he will have eternal life with God and with all his saints.
The Lord said that these signs will follow those who believe: "In my name they will drive out devils; they will speak with new tongues;
they will drive away serpents; and though they drink poison, it will not harm them; they will lay their hands on sick people, and they will be well."
These miracles were necessary at the beginning of Christianity, because through those signs the heathen people were turned to the faith.
The man who plants trees or plants waters them for as long as it takes until they are firmly rooted; once they are growing, he stops watering them:
In the same way Almighty God showed his miracles to the heathen people for as long as it took them to become believers. Once the faith had spread throughout the whole world, the miracles ceased.
But nevertheless God's church still daily performs spiritually the same miracles that the apostles then performed bodily.
When the priest christens the child, he drives the devil out of the child; for every heathen man belongs to the devil, but through holy baptism he belongs to God, if he keeps it.
He who gives up shameful stories and gossip and harmful scurrility, and occupies his mouth with God's praises and with prayers, then speaks with new tongues.
He who restrains the unruly or the impatient, and calms the bitterness of his heart, drives away the serpents, because he quenches the evils of his mind.
He who is enticed to fornication, and yet is not induced to commit it, drinks poison, but it does not harm him, if he flees to God with prayers.

If anyone is weakened in his undertaking and has grown slack in his good way of life, and someone then strengthens and raises him up with encouragement and the examples of good works, it is as if he laid his hands on a sick man and healed him.
The spiritual miracles are greater than the bodily ones were, because these miracles heal a person's soul, which is eternal, and the earlier signs healed the mortal body.
Both good men and evil worked the earlier miracles. Judas, who betrayed Christ, was evil, though he had earlier worked miracles through God's name.
Of such men Christ said in another place, "I say to you, many will say to me on that great day, 'Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name,
and did we not drive devils out of mad men, and do great mighty works in your name?' Then I will declare to them, 'I do not know you: depart from me, you workers of unrighteousness.'"
My brothers, do not love the miracles that can be shared by good and evil people alike. Love instead the signs that belong only to good people: the signs of true love and godliness.
The evil man does not have true love, and the good man is not without it.
These signs are hidden and free of danger, and the less glory they have among men, the greater the reward they have with God.
After these words the Ruling Lord was taken up to heaven, and he sits at the right hand of his Father.
We read in the old law that two men of God, Enoch and Elijah, were raised up to heaven without death. But they are only delaying death and will not escape it entirely.

They were taken up to the heaven of the air, not to the heaven of the firmament, and they live in some hidden land with great strength of body and soul, until they turn back again at the end of this world to oppose Antichrist, and suffer death.
Our Almighty Redeemer did not delay before death, but he overcame it by his resurrection, and showed his glory through his ascension to the highest throne.
We read of the prophet Elijah that angels carried him in a heavenly chariot, because the weakness of his nature needed something to carry him.
Our Redeemer Christ was not carried in a chariot or with the help of angels, because he who made all things was carried by his own power above all creatures.

The first man, Enoch, was carried to the heaven of the air, and Elijah was lifted up in a chariot. But the Almighty Saviour was neither carried nor lifted. He passed through the heavens of the sky by his own power.
It is for us to consider how chastity was growing, through the servants who were carried away and through the ascending Saviour.
Enoch was carried away, who had been begotten through sexual union, and who himself begot children through sexual union.
Elijah, who was begotten through sexual union, was carried in a chariot, but he did not beget anyone through sexual union, because he lived his life without a wife.
The Saviour ascended to heaven, who was not begotten through sexual union, nor did he himself beget children;
because he is the source and beginning of all chastity, and chastity is to him a very lovable virtue, which he showed when he chose a virgin as his mother.
And all the holy company that followed him lived in chastity, just as he said in a certain gospel, "He who comes to me cannot be my disciple unless he hates his wife."
The evangelist Mark wrote in this gospel that our Lord, after his ascension, sat at his Father's right hand;
and the first martyr, Stephen, said that he saw the heavens open, and the Savior standing at his Father's right hand.
Now the commentator says, "It is rightly said that he sat after his ascension, because a seat befits a judge."
Christ is the true judge, who judges and separates all things, now and also on the last day.
The martyr saw him standing, because he was his helper in the suffering of his martyrdom, and through his grace he was emboldened against the fierce persecutors who cruelly stoned him.
The end of this gospel is that Christ's apostles "went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word with the signs that followed."
The apostles, that is, God's heralds, went out across the whole world. Peter preached in the land of Judea, Paul among the heathen peoples, Andrew in Scythia,
John in Asia, Bartholomew in India, Matthew in Ethiopia, and so each of them in his own portion, and God's power was with them to carry out their preaching and countless miracles;
because Christ said, "You can do nothing without me." Again he said, "I am with you all days,
until the ending of this world," he who lives and reigns with the Almighty Father and the Holy Spirit forever into eternity. Amen.
